K2.text: Laura’s $300,000 buys ten Treasury holdings, one maturing before each $50,000 operating payment, and we never sell them early; the 2028 deposit fills any gap.

K3.text: Everything else goes into one world index fund for her facility contribution.

K4.text: We call our plan Caplet XR.

K5.text: It’s named after extended-release caplets, which release their dose on schedule and come labelled ‘do not crush’.

K6.text: Our ‘dose’ is Treasuries – Laura will, under our strategy, own the exact T-Bonds, T-Notes and Term Treasury ETFs she’ll need to fund her operating commitment.

K7.text: We chose Treasuries because her $50,000 payments are fixed and must be met with a high degree of certainty, and Treasuries pay fixed amounts on fixed dates, backed by the US government.

K8.text: At current Treasury prices her 10 operating payments would cost about $300,000 – which would generate roughly $200,000 in interest, therefore covering the $500,000 required in total – and whilst yields could of course look different by January 2027, we use these numbers as a guideline (and our plan is not dependent on them).

K9.text: In January 2027 we will use her $300,000 deposit to buy a ladder of 10 Treasury holdings (one maturing before each January from 2033 to 2042), and the 2028 deposit will fund any which the 2027 one couldn’t, if necessary.

K10.text: Each holding is bought so that what it repays, with its interest, meets that year’s $50,000.

K11.text: X is the Roman numeral for 10, and our XR (10 Rungs) will not be crushed: we won’t sell them before they mature.

K12.text: Bond prices will rise and fall before then, but a holding kept to maturity still pays what it was bought to pay, so those swings don’t affect the payments.

K13.text: The ladder is also her operating reserve.

K14.text: It is complete by January 2028 at the latest, five years before the first payment, so in 2033 there is nothing left to set aside or rearrange.

K15.text: From then on it releases its dose on schedule, like the caplet: one rung matures just before each January and pays that year’s $50,000, until the tenth pays the last one in 2042.

K16.text: Any funds from the 2027 and/or 2028 deposits not needed by the ladder will go into a world index fund (VT, Vanguard Total World Stock ETF).

K17.text: This is the money for her facility contribution in 2033 and for the flexibility she wants as the project develops.

K18.text: Because no operating payment depends on it, this money can take the risk of shares, which over long periods have grown faster than bonds.

K19.text: That suits Laura, who has taken thoughtful risks throughout her career.

K20.text: One fund holding thousands of companies across the world spreads that risk widely, costs little, and can be sold on any trading day when the money is needed.

K21.text: Shares can fall, and the fund could be worth less in 2033 than it cost, but a fall would reduce only what she can contribute.

K22.text: Our plan’s biggest strength, and our interpretation of ‘high degree of certainty’, is that – barring a US default – no operating payment is ever at risk, and they certainly never depend on a share price.

K23.text: Like the caplet it is named after, the plan works as long as nobody crushes it.

P411.2.text: On 4 August 2020 the same ten would have cost $470,217, more than both of Laura's deposits together.

P411.3.text: Monday 5 October 2026, two trading days before the team's orders filled, was the cheapest day for the ten since May 2002.

P411.4.text: Commissions came to $200, against a $37,625 swing in what the ten cost within 2026 ($325,563 on 27 February, $287,938 on 5 October).

P411.5.text: So the case is set in a rare year, and the plan is built to need the year, not the day: whatever the ten cost in January 2027, the first part of the 2028 deposit completes them and buys the extra Treasuries, and that keeps all ten paid even if cash waiting earns nothing unless yields fall about 3.6 points before January 2027.

P412.1.text: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline.

P412.2.text: This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan).

P412.3.text: The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?

F4.text: Laura Gao, a Wharton graduate who left tech to write and illustrate books (*The Wuhan I Know*, the graphic memoir *Messy Roots*).

F5.text: She is planning a creative residency in Taiwan for artists, writers and designers, opening in 2033.

F6.text: Money in: $300,000 at the start of 2027 and $150,000 at the start of 2028 (from book advances, speaking and licensing, so it depends on her career going well).

F7.text: Nothing else comes in or goes out before 2033.

F8.text: Money out: ten payments of $50,000, one at the start of each year from 2033 to 2042, to run the residency.

F9.text: These must be met "with a high degree of certainty", from the portfolio alone.

F10.text: After that she wants to give as much as she responsibly can towards the building (the "facility contribution"), while keeping flexibility.

F11.text: In 2031 she tells co-sponsors (other funders) a range in dollars and how confident she is.

F13.text: Caplet's plan (the IPS, frozen): the ten payments are bought with Treasuries in January 2027; the 2028 deposit first finishes that job, then most of it buys a Treasury fund that matures in late 2032 (the bottom of her range), and the rest buys VT, a world share fund (which sets the top).

F14.text: Half the shares are promised to no one; the other half moves into Treasuries before the 2031 meetings.

F15.text: The IPS names only two reasons to change the plan (l.17): a missed deposit or a Treasury default; "A fall in the market is not one of them."

F16.text: (Struck Wed 18 Nov evening, coherence reader 10, L1 and H2: "Only two things would change the plan:"; the two reasons are not the only ways a promise can fail, card Q109, NUMBERS 8u.)

F18.text: If yields fell 1 point before January 2027, the same ten would cost about $334,000; the 2028 deposit covers the difference.

F19.text: The first $39,162 of the 2028 deposit goes to the payments: $2,388 completes the ten (the top-up the IPS promised if yields fell), and $36,774 buys extra Treasuries so that the ten are paid even if the cash waiting between a bond's maturity and each 1 January earns nothing at all.

F20.text: The extra Treasuries are the part of the operating reserve, beyond the ten, that the case asks the team to recommend; never say they "complete" or "finish" the ten (coherence reader 6, Mon 16 Nov, H1).

F21.text: Why that matters: the bonds pay interest along the way, and one bond (February 2037) matures ten and a half months before the payment it funds (1 January 2038).

F22.text: That interest and that gap are where a "certain" plan could quietly depend on future interest rates.

F23.text: The extra Treasuries remove that dependence.

F41.text: Once both ends are owned, the range she states is certain; never put "certain" in the same sentence as the figures, and never "secured" for either end (funder test, Mon 16 Nov evening; coherence reader 6 and bond desk 4, M1).

F42.text: Her flexibility (the half of the shares promised to no one) is about $21,200 in January 2033, centrally; about $28,700 if you add whatever the funds pay above the top of the range.

F43.text: In a bad 1-in-20 future it is about $9,600.

F44.text: It is meant for three things the IPS names: building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar, or a co-sponsor falling short.

F45.text: A Taiwan dollar 10% stronger than in 2031 would need about $11,500 more; her flexibility covers that in about 93 of 100 model futures, and in about 98 of 100 two-year stretches of the real Taiwan dollar since 1983.

F46.text: Keep 30% of the shares back instead, and she could promise about $5,000 more (one $5,000 step; $10,000 before the Tue 17 Nov evening re-size), but her flexibility would cover a 10% stronger Taiwan dollar in only about half the futures.

F47.text: Keep 70% back, and she would promise about $10,000 less, with more flexibility and a narrower range.

F48.text: Each $5,000 more of promised top costs her about $5,300 of what she keeps.

F50.text: So the split decides what is promised and what stays hers, not how much there is.

F66.text: Laura is a graphic novelist and illustrator.

F67.text: Comic pages are drawn in pencil first, which can be rubbed out, then inked; only the ink is printed.

F68.text: In the report, ink is a dollar figure Laura already owns in Treasuries that will pay it on its date, and pencil is a figure no Treasury she owns will pay yet (her future income, the 2028 deposit before it arrives, the value of her shares before half of them move, interest on cash waiting, every forecast).

F69.text: She owns the shares; no Treasury pays their value.

F70.text: Laura only states a figure once it's inked.

F71.text: That is the IPS's own rule: "whatever figure you choose is money you already own".

F72.text: Say "owned" when you define it: most readers hear "inked" as "signed".

F73.text: Caplet's own words about the conceit: "It is intricate.

F75.text: It offers a startling new perspective."

F76.text: So it is not a word dropped in now and then: it is worked through, each turn showing something new.

F77.text: The turns you can use (all checked): - **One eraser, three lines.** A recession can shrink three pencil lines in the same downturn (never "rub out": IPS l.9 says "later and smaller"): her book advances, share prices, and co-sponsors' budgets (not always in the same months, and never every co-sponsor).

F78.text: That's why the promised money can't sit in pencil (coherence reader 6, Mon 16 Nov, M4). - **Finished before it's offered.** Comic publishers want several issues finished before a series is offered to shops ("three completed issues", Image, 2015).

F79.text: Laura's ten payments are bought in January 2027, six years before the first one goes out. - **The one line that waited.** From January 2027 to January 2028 the interest cash earns while it waits was the one pencil line in the payments; the extra Treasuries in January 2028 ink it.

F80.text: What comes back from them is worth about $46,600 in 2033 money if rates hold, all of it hers by 2042; if cash waiting earns nothing, none beyond the 0.5% margin for fund costs (never "most comes back"; coherence reader 8, M8).

F81.text: Publishers do something similar: they hold back part of an author's royalties against returns and release it once the risk passes. - **Ink only goes one way.** You can always add ink, but you can't take it off cleanly (a mistake is painted over and the original keeps the record).

F82.text: So every end of the range is rounded down, anything above the top goes to her flexibility, and half the shares stay pencil on purpose: co-sponsors never see them.

F83.text: Each $5,000 more she states costs her about $5,300 of what she keeps. - **Trim, bleed and safe area.** Printers run the art past the line where the page is cut, because the blade wanders, and keep the words well inside it.

F84.text: The stated top is the cut line; the 0.5% held back and the rounding down are the bleed; the bottom sits safely inside. - **Non-photo blue.** Artists drew construction lines in a light blue that the printing camera couldn't see.

F85.text: The report's models, the 7.5% and every median are like that: the judges see them, the co-sponsors in 2031 never will. - **The printed page.** Laura's words to co-sponsors have no comics words in them at all, because the printed page only shows ink. - **Erase every pencil line and the page still reads.** From January 2028, when the only pencil left is the shares (dated Wed 18 Nov evening, coherence reader 10, M4: the 2028 deposit is pencil until it arrives), if the shares went to zero, the ten payments wouldn't change and the range would be one figure, the bottom (no payout figure here, as in SKELETON and CONCEIT since Tue 17 Nov). - **Dot gain.** A press always prints a little darker than the file, so printers lighten the file first and the print lands where they want it.

F86.text: The funds' fee, the 0.5% held back and the rounding down are taken out before the range is stated, so the money comes out lighter than the figure she names only if the funds' other costs pass the room held back under the top (the 0.5% margin plus the rounding down, about 2% of what the fund pays, in all, never a year, on today's figures (Wed 18 Nov evening, bond desk 5, M1); never "the margin" for the whole room; "about 3%" before the Tue 17 Nov evening re-size, coherence reader 8, M2) (coherence reader 6, M1; bond desk 4, H1, Mon 16 Nov). - (Retired Tue 17 Nov after voice round 6: "let the ink dry" and the key plate needed decoding; do not use them.
